prompt: You want every new Pod created in the `payments` namespace to automatically receive an Istio sidecar proxy in sidecar mode. Which label must you set on the namespace?
options: `istio-injection=enabled`
`sidecar.istio.io/inject=true`
`istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient`
`istio.io/rev=enabled`
optionNotes: `istio-injection=enabled` on the namespace tells the istiod mutating webhook to inject the `istio-proxy` sidecar into every new Pod there, which is the correct answer.
`sidecar.istio.io/inject="true"` is a Pod-level label/annotation that opts a single Pod in (or out with `false`); it is not the namespace-wide switch.
`istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient` enrolls a namespace in ambient mode, which uses ztunnel instead of sidecars, so no sidecar is injected.
`istio.io/rev` selects a specific control plane revision, and its value must be a revision name such as `1-26`, not `enabled`.
explanation: Sidecar injection is driven by istiod's mutating admission webhook, which fires for Pods in namespaces labelled `istio-injection=enabled` (or `istio.io/rev=<revision>` for revisioned installs). Existing Pods are not modified; they must be restarted to pick up the sidecar. The Pod label `sidecar.istio.io/inject` only overrides the decision for one Pod, and the ambient label deliberately avoids sidecars.
example:
kubectl label namespace payments istio-injection=enabled
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n payments   # existing Pods need a restart
kubectl get pod -n payments -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.containers[*].name}'
# app istio-proxy
diagram:
flowchart LR
    NS["Namespace payments\nistio-injection=enabled"] --> API["kube-apiserver"]
    API -->|"Pod CREATE"| WH["istiod mutating webhook"]
    WH -->|"adds istio-init + istio-proxy"| POD["Pod app + sidecar"]
    POD -->|"xDS"| ISTIOD["istiod"]

prompt: A team runs `istioctl install` with no `--set profile` flag on a production cluster. Which built-in configuration profile is installed?
options: `default`
`demo`
`minimal`
`ambient`
optionNotes: `default` is what `istioctl install` uses when no profile is given; it installs istiod and an ingress gateway with production-oriented resource settings, so it is correct.
`demo` enables high levels of tracing and access logging and lowers resource requests for learning environments; it must be selected explicitly.
`minimal` installs only the control plane (istiod) with no gateways and must be requested explicitly.
`ambient` installs istiod plus ztunnel and the CNI node agent for ambient mode; it is never chosen implicitly.
explanation: `istioctl install` applies the `default` profile unless you override it with `--set profile=<name>` or an IstioOperator file. The `default` profile is recommended for production and includes istiod and the ingress gateway. `demo`, `minimal`, `ambient`, `empty`, `remote` and others exist but must be named explicitly.
example:
istioctl profile list
# ambient default demo empty minimal preview remote stable
istioctl install                       # == --set profile=default
istioctl install --set profile=demo -y  # for a lab
istioctl profile dump default | head
diagram:
flowchart TD
    I["istioctl install"] -->|"no profile flag"| D["default profile"]
    D --> C["istiod"]
    D --> G["istio-ingressgateway"]
    I -->|"--set profile=minimal"| M["istiod only"]
    I -->|"--set profile=ambient"| A["istiod + ztunnel + istio-cni"]

prompt: You have Istio 1.25 installed with revision `1-25` and install Istio 1.26 alongside it as revision `1-26` for a canary upgrade. How do you move the `orders` namespace to the new control plane?
options: Replace the namespace label `istio.io/rev=1-25` with `istio.io/rev=1-26`, then restart the workloads
Run `istioctl upgrade --revision 1-26` which migrates all namespaces at once
Edit the sidecar `istio-proxy` container image tag in each Deployment to 1.26
Set `istio-injection=enabled` on the namespace so it automatically follows the newest revision
optionNotes: Changing the `istio.io/rev` label to the new revision and restarting Pods re-injects them with the 1-26 proxy connected to the new istiod, which is the canary upgrade workflow.
`istioctl upgrade` performs an in-place upgrade of an existing revision; it is not how you migrate a namespace between coexisting revisions.
The proxy image is injected by the webhook, so hand-editing it is overwritten and does not switch the control plane the proxy talks to.
`istio-injection=enabled` targets the default (unrevisioned) webhook, and it cannot be combined with `istio.io/rev`; it does not track the newest revision.
explanation: With revision-based canary upgrades, multiple istiod control planes run side by side and each namespace selects one via the `istio.io/rev` label. To migrate, relabel the namespace to the new revision and restart the workloads so they are re-injected with proxies that connect to the new istiod. Once all namespaces are moved and verified, the old revision is uninstalled with `istioctl uninstall --revision 1-25`.
example:
istioctl install --set revision=1-26 -y
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=istiod   # istiod-1-25 and istiod-1-26
kubectl label ns orders istio.io/rev=1-26 --overwrite
kubectl rollout restart deploy -n orders
istioctl proxy-status                              # proxies now report 1-26
istioctl uninstall --revision 1-25 -y             # after all namespaces move
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["istiod 1-25"] ---|"xDS"| P1["Pods in ns billing\nistio.io/rev=1-25"]
    B["istiod 1-26"] ---|"xDS"| P2["Pods in ns orders\nistio.io/rev=1-26"]
    L["relabel + rollout restart"] -->|"moves ns orders"| B

prompt: A `VirtualService` routes 90% of traffic to subset `v1` and 10% to subset `v2` of the `reviews` service, but `istioctl analyze` reports an error and requests fail with 503. What is most likely missing?
options: A `DestinationRule` for `reviews` that defines the `v1` and `v2` subsets with label selectors
A `Gateway` resource bound to the `VirtualService`
A `ServiceEntry` registering `reviews` in the mesh
A `PeerAuthentication` with mode `PERMISSIVE`
optionNotes: Subsets are declared in a `DestinationRule` that maps each subset name to Pod labels such as `version: v1`; without it Envoy has no cluster for `reviews|v1` and returns 503, so this is correct.
A `Gateway` is only needed for traffic entering from outside the mesh; in-mesh routing between services works with just a `VirtualService` and `DestinationRule`.
`reviews` is a regular Kubernetes Service and is already in the mesh registry; `ServiceEntry` is for hosts outside Kubernetes.
mTLS mode does not affect subset resolution; a missing subset produces a 503 regardless of authentication settings.
explanation: `VirtualService` references subsets by name, but the subsets themselves (and their label selectors, load balancing and TLS settings) are defined in a `DestinationRule`. If the `DestinationRule` is missing, istiod cannot generate the `outbound|9080|v1|reviews...` cluster, `istioctl analyze` emits an IST0101 referenced-subset error, and Envoy returns 503 NR/NC. Gateways, ServiceEntries and PeerAuthentication address different concerns.
example:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: reviews
spec:
  host: reviews
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels: {version: v1}
  - name: v2
    labels: {version: v2}
---
# VirtualService: route: [{destination: {host: reviews, subset: v1}, weight: 90}, {destination: {host: reviews, subset: v2}, weight: 10}]
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["client sidecar"] --> VS["VirtualService reviews\n90/10 weights"]
    VS -->|"subset v1"| DR["DestinationRule reviews"]
    VS -->|"subset v2"| DR
    DR -->|"labels version=v1"| P1["reviews-v1 Pods"]
    DR -->|"labels version=v2"| P2["reviews-v2 Pods"]

prompt: Name the `istioctl` subcommand that inspects your cluster's Istio configuration and reports potential problems such as a `VirtualService` referencing an undefined subset (single word after `istioctl`).
explanation: `istioctl analyze` runs a set of analyzers against the live cluster (or local YAML files with `--use-kubeconfig=false`) and prints messages like `Error [IST0101] Referenced host+subset not found`. It is the first tool to reach for when routing does not behave as expected. `istioctl proxy-status` and `proxy-config` inspect Envoy state instead of configuration validity.
example:
istioctl analyze -n bookinfo
# Error [IST0101] (VirtualService bookinfo/reviews) Referenced host+subset in destinationrule not found: "reviews+v3"
istioctl analyze --all-namespaces
istioctl analyze --use-kubeconfig=false virtual-service.yaml   # offline lint
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["istioctl analyze"] --> K["reads Istio CRs from cluster"]
    K --> AN["runs analyzers"]
    AN --> M1["IST0101 subset not found"]
    AN --> M2["IST0102 namespace not injected"]
    AN --> OK["No validation issues found"]

prompt: Which values are valid for `spec.mtls.mode` in an Istio `PeerAuthentication` resource? (Select all that apply.)
options: `STRICT`
`PERMISSIVE`
`DISABLE`
`MUTUAL`
`SIMPLE`
`ISTIO_MUTUAL`
optionNotes: `STRICT` is valid: the workload accepts only mutual TLS connections.
`PERMISSIVE` is valid and the default: both plaintext and mTLS are accepted.
`DISABLE` is valid: mTLS is turned off and only plaintext is accepted.
`MUTUAL` is a `DestinationRule` client-side TLS mode for presenting your own certificates, not a `PeerAuthentication` mode.
`SIMPLE` is a `DestinationRule` TLS mode for one-way TLS to an upstream, not a `PeerAuthentication` mode.
`ISTIO_MUTUAL` is a `DestinationRule` TLS mode that uses Istio-issued certs; it is not a valid `PeerAuthentication` mode.
explanation: `PeerAuthentication` controls what the receiving sidecar accepts and supports `UNSET`, `DISABLE`, `PERMISSIVE` and `STRICT`. `SIMPLE`, `MUTUAL` and `ISTIO_MUTUAL` (plus `DISABLE`) belong to `DestinationRule.spec.trafficPolicy.tls.mode`, which governs the client side of the connection. Mixing these two APIs up is a common exam trap.
example:
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: istio-system   # mesh-wide when placed in the root namespace
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: STRICT            # STRICT | PERMISSIVE | DISABLE | UNSET
diagram:
flowchart LR
    PA["PeerAuthentication\nserver side"] --> S["STRICT mTLS only"]
    PA --> P["PERMISSIVE mTLS or plaintext"]
    PA --> D["DISABLE plaintext only"]
    DR["DestinationRule tls.mode\nclient side"] --> IM["ISTIO_MUTUAL"]
    DR --> MU["MUTUAL"]
    DR --> SI["SIMPLE"]

prompt: With a `PeerAuthentication` mode of `PERMISSIVE`, a sidecar accepts both mutual-TLS connections from mesh peers and plaintext connections from clients without a sidecar.
explanation: `PERMISSIVE` is Istio's default and exists precisely to ease migration: the server-side proxy accepts mTLS and plaintext at the same time, so legacy or not-yet-injected workloads keep working. Once every client is in the mesh you switch to `STRICT`, which rejects plaintext.
example:
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: legacy
spec:
  mtls:
    mode: PERMISSIVE   # accept mTLS and plaintext during migration
# verify: curl from a non-injected pod still succeeds
diagram:
flowchart LR
    M["mesh client with sidecar"] -->|"mTLS"| S["server sidecar\nPERMISSIVE"]
    L["legacy client no sidecar"] -->|"plaintext"| S
    S --> APP["app container"]
    L2["legacy client"] -.->|"plaintext rejected"| ST["server sidecar\nSTRICT"]

prompt: You apply a `RequestAuthentication` for the `api` workload that points at your identity provider's JWKS. Requests carrying no `Authorization` header still succeed. Why?
options: `RequestAuthentication` only rejects requests with an invalid token; requests with no token are accepted unless an `AuthorizationPolicy` requires a principal
The JWKS URI is unreachable, so istiod silently disables validation
`RequestAuthentication` needs `mtls.mode: STRICT` before it takes effect
The resource must be created in `istio-system` to be enforced
optionNotes: This is correct: `RequestAuthentication` validates tokens that are present, and a request with no token passes with an empty principal; enforcing presence requires an `AuthorizationPolicy` with `requestPrincipals: ["*"]`.
An unreachable JWKS makes valid tokens fail, not missing tokens pass; and Istio does not silently disable validation.
JWT request authentication is independent of peer mTLS mode.
Placing the policy in the root namespace makes it mesh-wide, but a namespaced `RequestAuthentication` with a selector is enforced just fine.
explanation: `RequestAuthentication` defines how to validate JWTs (issuer, JWKS), and rejects requests whose token is invalid, but it does not require that a token be present. To mandate authentication, add an `AuthorizationPolicy` whose `from.source.requestPrincipals` is `["*"]`, which denies any request that has no validated principal. This two-resource pattern is the standard way to protect a workload with JWT.
example:
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: RequestAuthentication
metadata: {name: api-jwt, namespace: prod}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  jwtRules:
  - issuer: "https://issuer.example.com"
    jwksUri: "https://issuer.example.com/.well-known/jwks.json"
---
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata: {name: api-require-jwt, namespace: prod}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: api}}
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from:
    - source: {requestPrincipals: ["*"]}   # token must be present and valid
diagram:
flowchart TD
    R["incoming request"] --> RA["RequestAuthentication"]
    RA -->|"invalid JWT"| D1["401 rejected"]
    RA -->|"valid JWT"| AP["AuthorizationPolicy\nrequestPrincipals *"]
    RA -->|"no JWT, empty principal"| AP
    AP -->|"principal present"| OK["allowed"]
    AP -->|"no principal"| D2["403 denied"]

prompt: A workload has one `AuthorizationPolicy` with `action: ALLOW` permitting `GET` from the `frontend` service account, and a second with `action: DENY` blocking path `/admin`. A request from `frontend` sends `POST /orders`. What happens?
options: Denied, because an ALLOW policy exists and none of its rules match the request
Allowed, because the request does not match the DENY policy
Allowed, because the ALLOW policy matches the source `frontend`
Denied, because DENY policies are evaluated last and reject anything not explicitly listed
optionNotes: Correct: Istio first evaluates CUSTOM, then DENY, then ALLOW; once at least one ALLOW policy targets a workload, any request that matches no ALLOW rule is rejected.
Not matching a DENY rule only means the request is not denied at that stage; it must still match an ALLOW rule when ALLOW policies exist.
The ALLOW rule requires both the `frontend` principal and the `GET` method; a `POST` does not satisfy the rule.
DENY policies are evaluated before ALLOW, and they never reject unlisted requests; only the presence of ALLOW policies produces implicit denial.
explanation: Istio's authorization engine evaluates policies in the order CUSTOM, DENY, ALLOW. If a DENY rule matches, the request is rejected; otherwise, if any ALLOW policies apply to the workload, the request must match one of them or it is denied. Here `/orders` is not blocked by DENY, but the ALLOW rule only covers `GET`, so `POST /orders` matches no ALLOW rule and is rejected with 403 `RBAC: access denied`.
example:
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata: {name: allow-frontend-get, namespace: shop}
spec:
  selector: {matchLabels: {app: orders}}
  action: ALLOW
  rules:
  - from: [{source: {principals: ["cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/frontend"]}}]
    to:   [{operation: {methods: ["GET"]}}]
# POST /orders from frontend -> 403 RBAC: access denied
diagram:
flowchart TD
    R["request POST /orders"] --> C["CUSTOM policies"]
    C --> D["DENY policies\npath /admin"]
    D -->|"no match"| A["ALLOW policies exist?"]
    A -->|"yes, rule GET only"| M["any ALLOW rule match?"]
    M -->|"no"| X["403 denied"]
    M -->|"yes"| OK["allowed"]
    A -->|"no ALLOW policies"| OK

prompt: Istio's SPIFFE identity for a workload has the form `spiffe://<trust-domain>/ns/<namespace>/sa/<name>`. Which Kubernetes resource kind supplies the `<name>` part of that identity?
explanation: On Kubernetes, Istio derives each workload's identity from the Pod's `ServiceAccount`; the certificate issued by istiod carries the SPIFFE URI `spiffe://cluster.local/ns/<namespace>/sa/<serviceaccount>` as a SAN. Deployment or Pod names are not part of the identity, which is why `AuthorizationPolicy.principals` are written in `ns/sa` form and why workloads should not share the `default` ServiceAccount.
example:
kubectl get pod frontend-7d9 -o jsonpath='{.spec.serviceAccountName}'
# frontend
istioctl proxy-config secret frontend-7d9 -o json | jq -r '.dynamicActiveSecrets[0].secret.tlsCertificate.certificateChain.inlineBytes' | base64 -d | openssl x509 -noout -text | grep spiffe
# URI:spiffe://cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/frontend
diagram:
flowchart LR
    SA["ServiceAccount frontend\nns shop"] --> POD["Pod frontend"]
    POD -->|"CSR via SDS"| ISTIOD["istiod CA"]
    ISTIOD -->|"X.509 cert with SAN"| ID["spiffe://cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/frontend"]
    ID --> AP["AuthorizationPolicy principals"]

prompt: To test how `checkout` copes with a slow dependency, you want 50% of requests to `inventory` to be delayed by 5 seconds before being forwarded. Where do you configure this?
options: In a `VirtualService` for `inventory` using `fault.delay` with `percentage.value: 50` and `fixedDelay: 5s`
In a `DestinationRule` for `inventory` using `outlierDetection.baseEjectionTime: 5s`
In a `PeerAuthentication` using `mtls.mode: PERMISSIVE` with a `delay` field
In an `EnvoyFilter` that patches the `inventory` Deployment's readiness probe
optionNotes: Correct: HTTP fault injection lives under `VirtualService.spec.http[].fault`, where `delay` and `abort` faults can be applied to a percentage of matched requests.
`outlierDetection` is a circuit-breaker that ejects unhealthy endpoints; it does not delay requests.
`PeerAuthentication` only configures mTLS and has no `delay` field.
`EnvoyFilter` is a low-level escape hatch and readiness probes are Kubernetes constructs; neither is the Istio way to inject latency.
explanation: Fault injection is a `VirtualService` feature: the `fault` block supports `delay` (add latency) and `abort` (return an HTTP or gRPC error) with a `percentage`. Because it is applied by the client-side Envoy, no application code or chaos tool is needed. `DestinationRule` handles resilience settings like outlier detection and connection pools, not faults.
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["checkout app"] --> E["checkout sidecar"]
    E -->|"50% of requests"| D["delay 5s"]
    E -->|"50% of requests"| I["inventory"]
    D --> I
    VS["VirtualService fault.delay"] -.->|"configures"| E

prompt: You configure a `VirtualService` route with `mirror: {host: reviews, subset: v2}` and `mirrorPercentage: {value: 100}`. Which statement about the mirrored traffic is correct?
options: Every request is copied to `reviews` v2 asynchronously and its response is discarded; the client only sees the primary route's response
Requests are load-balanced 50/50 between the primary destination and the mirror
The client receives whichever response arrives first from the primary or the mirror
Mirroring requires `retries` to be configured so the mirror can be retried on failure
optionNotes: Correct: mirroring is fire-and-forget; Envoy sends a copy of the request to the mirror target, ignores its response, and the primary destination's response is returned to the caller.
Mirroring never affects the primary routing weights; use `weight` on multiple `route.destination` entries for traffic splitting.
There is no racing of responses; the mirror's response is always dropped.
Retries and mirroring are independent features; mirrored requests are not retried.
explanation: Traffic mirroring (shadowing) lets you test a new version with real production traffic at zero risk. The sidecar copies each matched request to the mirror destination, with the `Host` header suffixed `-shadow`, and does not wait for or use its response. `mirrorPercentage` (default 100) controls how many requests are copied. Because the mirror response is discarded, mirror failures never affect users.
example:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata: {name: reviews}
spec:
  hosts: [reviews]
  http:
  - route:
    - destination: {host: reviews, subset: v1}
      weight: 100
    mirror: {host: reviews, subset: v2}
    mirrorPercentage: {value: 100}   # copy all requests to v2, ignore replies
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["client"] --> S["client sidecar"]
    S -->|"primary request"| V1["reviews v1"]
    V1 -->|"response returned"| S
    S -->|"mirrored copy, Host reviews-shadow"| V2["reviews v2"]
    V2 -.->|"response discarded"| X["dropped"]

prompt: Your mesh has `outboundTrafficPolicy.mode: REGISTRY_ONLY`. Sidecars now block calls to `api.stripe.com`. Which resource lets workloads reach that external host while keeping the policy in place?
options: A `ServiceEntry` for `api.stripe.com` with `location: MESH_EXTERNAL` and `resolution: DNS`
A `VirtualService` with `hosts: [api.stripe.com]` and a passthrough route
A `Gateway` resource selecting the ingress gateway on port 443
An `AuthorizationPolicy` with `action: ALLOW` for host `api.stripe.com`
optionNotes: Correct: `ServiceEntry` adds external hosts to Istio's service registry so `REGISTRY_ONLY` allows them, and `resolution: DNS` tells Envoy to resolve the hostname.
A `VirtualService` can only route to hosts already in the registry; without a `ServiceEntry` the host is unknown and still blocked.
`Gateway` handles traffic entering or leaving through a gateway proxy and does not register an external service.
`AuthorizationPolicy` governs inbound access to workloads; it does not control the outbound registry check.
explanation: `REGISTRY_ONLY` makes sidecars reject traffic to any destination not in the Istio service registry (the default `ALLOW_ANY` passes unknown hosts through). `ServiceEntry` is how you add external hosts, IP ranges or VMs to that registry; once added you can also attach `VirtualService` timeouts and retries, `DestinationRule` TLS origination, and telemetry to the external call.
example:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: ServiceEntry
metadata: {name: stripe}
spec:
  hosts: [api.stripe.com]
  location: MESH_EXTERNAL
  resolution: DNS
  ports:
  - {number: 443, name: https, protocol: TLS}
# istioctl install --set meshConfig.outboundTrafficPolicy.mode=REGISTRY_ONLY
diagram:
flowchart LR
    APP["app"] --> SC["sidecar\nREGISTRY_ONLY"]
    SC -->|"host in registry?"| REG["Istio service registry"]
    SE["ServiceEntry api.stripe.com"] --> REG
    REG -->|"yes"| EXT["api.stripe.com"]
    REG -->|"no"| BH["BlackHoleCluster 502"]

prompt: Which statements accurately describe Istio's ambient mode data plane? (Select all that apply.)
options: `ztunnel` runs as a per-node DaemonSet and provides L4 mTLS and TCP authorization without sidecars
Waypoint proxies are Envoy Deployments that are only needed when L7 features such as HTTP routing or `AuthorizationPolicy` on HTTP attributes are required
Each Pod still receives an injected `istio-proxy` container, but it is configured for L4 only
A namespace is added to ambient mode with the label `istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient` and Pods do not need to be restarted
Ambient mode requires the Kubernetes cluster to run with `hostNetwork` enabled on all workloads
optionNotes: Correct: ztunnel is a Rust-based node-level proxy that handles mTLS (HBONE), L4 authorization and TCP telemetry for all Pods on the node.
Correct: waypoints are optional, per-namespace or per-service Envoy proxies that add the L7 layer only where you opt in.
Incorrect: ambient mode has no sidecar container at all; that is its main difference from sidecar mode.
Correct: enrolling is a namespace label change handled by the CNI node agent, and running Pods are captured without restart.
Incorrect: ambient uses the `istio-cni` node agent to redirect Pod traffic to ztunnel; workloads keep their normal Pod networking.
explanation: Ambient mode splits Istio's data plane into two layers: ztunnel (a per-node secure overlay handling identity, mTLS and L4 policy) and optional waypoint proxies (Envoy) for L7 features. Because there are no sidecars, Pods are enrolled by labelling the namespace and need no restart or resource changes. Sidecar-specific ideas like an injected `istio-proxy` container do not apply.
example:
istioctl install --set profile=ambient -y
kubectl label namespace shop istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient   # no pod restart
kubectl get pods -n istio-system -l app=ztunnel               # one per node
istioctl waypoint apply -n shop --enroll-namespace              # add L7 only if needed
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["Pod a"] -->|"redirected by istio-cni"| Z1["ztunnel node 1\nL4 mTLS"]
    Z1 -->|"HBONE"| W["waypoint proxy\nL7 optional"]
    W --> Z2["ztunnel node 2"]
    Z1 -->|"HBONE, no L7 needed"| Z2
    Z2 --> B["Pod b"]

prompt: An ambient-mode namespace `shop` already has a waypoint named `waypoint` deployed. HTTP `AuthorizationPolicy` rules for the `orders` service are still not enforced. What is the most likely cause?
options: The namespace or service has not been labelled `istio.io/use-waypoint=waypoint`, so traffic bypasses the waypoint
Waypoints only support TCP; HTTP policies require sidecar mode
The `AuthorizationPolicy` must be in `istio-system` to reach a waypoint
ztunnel must be restarted after a waypoint is created
optionNotes: Correct: deploying a waypoint does nothing until workloads are enrolled by setting `istio.io/use-waypoint` on the namespace (or on individual Services or Pods); without it ztunnel sends traffic directly to the destination.
Waypoints are full Envoy L7 proxies; supporting HTTP routing and policy is their entire purpose.
Policies are namespaced and target workloads in the same namespace; the root namespace is only for mesh-wide defaults.
ztunnel reads waypoint bindings dynamically from istiod; no restart is involved.
explanation: In ambient mode, creating a waypoint (`istioctl waypoint apply` or a Gateway with `gatewayClassName: istio-waypoint`) only provisions the proxy. Traffic is routed through it only for namespaces, Services or Pods carrying the `istio.io/use-waypoint: <name>` label, which `--enroll-namespace` sets for you. Until then, L7 features such as HTTP `AuthorizationPolicy`, `VirtualService` header routing and HTTP telemetry are not applied, while ztunnel still enforces L4 policy and mTLS.
example:
istioctl waypoint apply -n shop --enroll-namespace
# equivalent manual step:
kubectl label ns shop istio.io/use-waypoint=waypoint
kubectl get gateway -n shop
# NAME       CLASS            PROGRAMMED
# waypoint   istio-waypoint   True
istioctl ztunnel-config workload -n shop   # WAYPOINT column now shows shop/waypoint
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["client Pod"] --> Z["ztunnel"]
    Z -->|"ns labelled use-waypoint"| W["waypoint Envoy\nHTTP AuthorizationPolicy"]
    W --> O["orders Pod"]
    Z -.->|"no label, L4 only"| O
    L["istio.io/use-waypoint=waypoint"] -.-> Z

prompt: To add existing running Pods to an Istio ambient-mode mesh, you must restart them after labelling their namespace, just as you would for sidecar injection.
explanation: This is a sidecar-mode habit that does not carry over. In ambient mode the `istio-cni` node agent reprograms traffic redirection for Pods in a namespace as soon as it is labelled `istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient`, so running Pods are captured by ztunnel immediately with no restart and no change to the Pod spec. Only sidecar mode needs a restart, because the sidecar container is injected at Pod creation time.
example:
kubectl label ns shop istio.io/dataplane-mode=ambient
istioctl ztunnel-config workload -n shop
# NAMESPACE  POD NAME        PROTOCOL  WAYPOINT

An annotation `sidecar.istio.io/accessLog: /dev/stdout` on the namespace
A `DestinationRule` in `checkout` with `trafficPolicy.logging: enabled`

prompt: Calls to `ratings` occasionally fail with transient 503s. You add `retries: {attempts: 3, perTryTimeout: 2s, retryOn: "5xx,reset"}` to the `VirtualService` and also set `timeout: 5s` on the route. What is the maximum time a single client request can take before Envoy gives up?
options: About 5 seconds, because the route `timeout` caps the total including all retries
About 6 seconds, because three retries at 2 seconds each are allowed
About 8 seconds, because the original attempt plus three retries each get 2 seconds
Unlimited, because retries reset the route timeout each time
optionNotes: Correct: the route-level `timeout` is the overall budget for the request; `perTryTimeout` bounds each individual attempt, and retries stop once the overall timeout is hit.
Multiplying attempts by `perTryTimeout` ignores the overall `timeout`, which is shorter here.
Adding the original attempt to the retries still exceeds the overall 5s timeout, which wins.
The route timeout is not reset by retries; it is a hard ceiling for the whole request.
explanation: In a `VirtualService`, `timeout` applies to the entire request including retries, while `retries.perTryTimeout` limits each attempt and must be less than or equal to the overall timeout. `retryOn` selects the conditions (Envoy retry policies such as `5xx`, `reset`, `connect-failure`, `retriable-status-codes`). Istio's default is 2 retries on `connect-failure,refused-stream,unavailable,cancelled,retriable-status-codes` with no default overall timeout.
example:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata: {name: ratings}
spec:
  hosts: [ratings]
  http:
  - route:
    - destination: {host: ratings, subset: v1}
    timeout: 5s               # overall budget
    retries:
      attempts: 3
      perTryTimeout: 2s       # per attempt, must be <= timeout
      retryOn: 5xx,reset
diagram:
flowchart LR
    R["request"] --> T1["try 1 up to 2s"]
    T1 -->|"503"| T2["try 2 up to 2s"]
    T2 -->|"503"| T3["try 3 cut short"]
    T3 --> X["overall timeout 5s reached\n504 returned"]
    T1 -->|"200"| OK["success"]

prompt: The `ratings` service has three Pods and one of them keeps returning 5xx. You want Envoy to stop sending traffic to a Pod after 5 consecutive 5xx responses and keep it out of rotation for at least 30 seconds. Which `DestinationRule` field configures this?
options: `trafficPolicy.outlierDetection`
`trafficPolicy.connectionPool.http.maxRequestsPerConnection`
`trafficPolicy.loadBalancer.simple: LEAST_REQUEST`
`trafficPolicy.tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL`
optionNotes: `outlierDetection` is Envoy's passive health checking (circuit breaker per host); `consecutive5xxErrors`, `interval`, and `baseEjectionTime` implement exactly this behaviour, so this is correct.
`maxRequestsPerConnection` bounds how many requests are sent over one keep-alive connection; it does not react to error responses.
`LEAST_REQUEST` changes which healthy endpoint is picked; it still routes to a failing Pod because the load balancer does not track 5xx responses.
`ISTIO_MUTUAL` selects mTLS for upstream connections and has nothing to do with ejecting unhealthy endpoints.
explanation: Outlier detection is Istio's implementation of per-endpoint circuit breaking: Envoy tracks consecutive errors per host and temporarily ejects the host from the load-balancing pool. `baseEjectionTime` is multiplied by the number of times the host has been ejected, and `maxEjectionPercent` caps how much of the pool can be removed at once.
example:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: ratings
spec:
  host: ratings.default.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 5
      interval: 10s
      baseEjectionTime: 30s
      maxEjectionPercent: 50

flowchart LR
    C["client sidecar"] --> P1["ratings pod 1"]
    C --> P2["ratings pod 2"]
    C -.->|"ejected 30s after 5x 5xx"| P3["ratings pod 3"]
    OD["outlierDetection"] --> C

prompt: A load test against `checkout` shows the sidecar returning HTTP 503 with the response flag `UO` (upstream overflow) even though the `checkout` Pods are healthy. Which `DestinationRule` setting is most likely limiting the traffic?
options: `trafficPolicy.connectionPool` limits such as `http.http1MaxPendingRequests` or `tcp.maxConnections`
`trafficPolicy.outlierDetection.maxEjectionPercent` set too high
`spec.subsets` missing a `version` label
`trafficPolicy.loadBalancer.consistentHash` without a hash key
optionNotes: Connection pool settings are Envoy circuit breaker thresholds; when they are exceeded Envoy fails fast with 503 and the `UO` flag, so this is correct.
Outlier detection ejects hosts based on errors and produces `UH` (no healthy upstream) rather than `UO`; the Pods are healthy here anyway.
A missing subset label would produce `NR`/`NC` style routing errors or `503 no healthy upstream`, not an overflow flag.
A `consistentHash` policy without a key is rejected by validation; it does not cause overflow.
explanation: `connectionPool` maps to Envoy circuit breakers: `tcp.maxConnections`, `http.http1MaxPendingRequests`, and `http.http2MaxRequests`. When a threshold is hit Envoy does not queue; it returns 503 immediately and marks the access log with `UO`. Raising the limits or scaling the service fixes it.
example:
# access log excerpt from the client sidecar
[2026-09-12T10:01:02Z] "POST /pay HTTP/1.1" 503 UO ... "checkout.shop.svc.cluster.local"

spec:
  host: checkout
  trafficPolicy:
    connectionPool:
      tcp:
        maxConnections: 100
      http:
        http1MaxPendingRequests: 100
        http2MaxRequests: 1000
diagram:
flowchart LR
    A["load test"] --> S["client sidecar"]
    S -->|"within pool limits"| U["checkout pods"]
    S -->|"over limit: 503 UO"| X["fail fast"]
    DR["DestinationRule connectionPool"] --> S

prompt: Your mesh runs in `STRICT` mTLS. A platform team adds a `DestinationRule` for `orders` with `trafficPolicy.tls.mode: SIMPLE` to "enable TLS". Immediately, all calls to `orders` fail. What went wrong?
options: `SIMPLE` makes the client sidecar originate plain TLS without an Istio client certificate, so the `orders` sidecar rejects the connection under `STRICT` mTLS; `ISTIO_MUTUAL` was needed
`SIMPLE` disables TLS entirely, so plaintext is sent to a STRICT server
`SIMPLE` is only valid inside `Gateway` resources and is silently ignored on a `DestinationRule`
The `DestinationRule` needs a `subsets` entry before `trafficPolicy.tls` takes effect
optionNotes: Correct: `SIMPLE` means one-way TLS using no client certificate (or a user-supplied one), which fails the mTLS handshake required by the STRICT `PeerAuthentication`; `ISTIO_MUTUAL` uses the automatically provisioned Istio certificates.
`DISABLE` is the mode that sends plaintext; `SIMPLE` does originate TLS, just without the mesh identity.
`SIMPLE` is valid on `DestinationRule` and commonly used for TLS origination to external hosts via a `ServiceEntry`.
`trafficPolicy` at the top level applies to all traffic to the host; subsets are optional.
explanation: `DestinationRule` TLS modes control what the client sidecar originates: `DISABLE` (plaintext), `SIMPLE` (one-way TLS), `MUTUAL` (mTLS with user-provided certs), and `ISTIO_MUTUAL` (mTLS with Istio-issued SPIFFE certs). Under automatic mTLS you normally omit the field; setting `SIMPLE` or `DISABLE` for an in-mesh host is a classic cause of `503 UF` handshake failures.
example:
# what the team wrote (breaks STRICT mTLS)
trafficPolicy:
  tls:
    mode: SIMPLE

# correct for an in-mesh service (or omit entirely for auto mTLS)
trafficPolicy:
  tls:
    mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL

istioctl x describe pod orders-7c9f...   # shows effective TLS mode
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["client sidecar\ntls.mode SIMPLE"] -->|"TLS, no client cert"| S["orders sidecar\nPeerAuthentication STRICT"]
    S -->|"handshake rejected"| E["503 UF"]
    C2["client sidecar\nISTIO_MUTUAL"] -->|"mTLS with SPIFFE cert"| S

Acting as the certificate authority that signs workload certificates via the SDS flow
Forwarding application data-plane traffic between sidecars
Running the mutating admission webhook that injects sidecars
Storing per-request access logs for later querying

Correct: istiod embeds Citadel, which issues SPIFFE certificates to proxies over the Secret Discovery Service.
Wrong: data-plane traffic flows only between Envoy proxies (or ztunnel); istiod is never on the request path.

prompt: You have a `VirtualService` with two routes: the first matches `headers: {end-user: {exact: jason}}` and sends to subset `v2`; the second has no `match` and sends to `v1`. A developer reorders the rules so the catch-all comes first. What happens to requests from `jason`?
options: They all go to `v1`, because routes are evaluated top to bottom and the first match wins
They still go to `v2`, because more specific matches are always evaluated before catch-all routes
The `VirtualService` is rejected by the validating webhook for having an unreachable route
Traffic is split 50/50 between `v1` and `v2`
optionNotes: Correct: Istio evaluates `http` routes in order and uses the first whose `match` succeeds; a catch-all placed first shadows every later route.
Istio does not sort by specificity; ordering in the resource is significant.
Validation does not detect unreachable routes, although `istioctl analyze` may warn about them (IST0104 style messages).
Weighted splitting only happens within a single route's `route` list, not across separate rules.
explanation: In a `VirtualService`, the `http` (and `tcp`, `tls`) routing rules are an ordered list. The proxy walks them top down and applies the first rule whose match conditions are satisfied, so the most specific rules must appear before any default rule.
example:
spec:
  hosts: [reviews]
  http:
  - match:
    - headers:
        end-user:
          exact: jason
    route:
    - destination: {host: reviews, subset: v2}
  - route:                      # catch-all must be last
    - destination: {host: reviews, subset: v1}

prompt: A cluster with 800 services has sidecars whose memory keeps growing, and `istioctl proxy-config clusters` on a Pod in the `billing` namespace lists every service in the mesh. `billing` only ever calls services in `billing` and `istio-system`. Which resource reduces the configuration pushed to those sidecars?
options: A `Sidecar` resource in `billing` with `egress.hosts` set to `./*` and `istio-system/*`
A `ServiceEntry` in `billing` with `exportTo: ["."]`
A `DestinationRule` in `billing` with `exportTo: ["."]`
An `AuthorizationPolicy` in `billing` allowing only `billing` and `istio-system` sources
optionNotes: Correct: the `Sidecar` resource limits which hosts a proxy is configured to reach; `./*` means the same namespace and `istio-system/*` adds the control plane namespace, so xDS payloads shrink dramatically.
`exportTo` on a `ServiceEntry` restricts who sees that entry, but Kubernetes Services in other namespaces are still pushed to `billing`.
`exportTo` on a `DestinationRule` only scopes that one rule; it does not remove clusters for other services.
`AuthorizationPolicy` governs inbound access at the server; it does not change what outbound clusters and routes the client sidecar receives.
explanation: By default istiod pushes configuration for every service in the mesh to every sidecar, which scales poorly. A `Sidecar` resource (one per namespace without a `workloadSelector` acts as the namespace default) trims the egress hosts, cutting both memory usage in Envoy and push time in istiod. A mesh-wide default can be placed in the root namespace.
example:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: Sidecar
metadata:
  name: default
  namespace: billing
spec:
  egress:
  - hosts:
    - "./*"
    - "istio-system/*"

istioctl proxy-config clusters billing-api-xyz.billing | wc -l   # far fewer

prompt: An `AuthorizationPolicy` with `action: DENY` targets `payments` and denies requests whose `source.namespaces` is `dev`. A second policy with `action: ALLOW` explicitly allows the `dev` namespace to call `payments`. What does a request from `dev` receive?
options: It is denied, because `DENY` policies are evaluated before `ALLOW` policies and a matching deny always wins
It is allowed, because the more recently applied policy takes precedence
It is allowed, because `ALLOW` policies override `DENY` when both match
istiod refuses to apply conflicting policies and logs a validation error
optionNotes: Correct: Istio evaluates `CUSTOM`, then `DENY`, then `ALLOW`; if any `DENY` rule matches the request is rejected regardless of allow rules.
Creation time has no bearing on precedence; only the action type and match do.
This is reversed; deny is checked first and short-circuits.
Policies are independent resources and do not conflict from the validator's point of view.
explanation: Authorization evaluation order is: `CUSTOM` policies (external authz) first, then `DENY`, then `ALLOW`. A request is rejected if any `DENY` matches; otherwise, if there are no `ALLOW` policies it is allowed, and if there are, it must match at least one. This makes `DENY` a safe way to carve exceptions out of broad allows.
example:
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: AuthorizationPolicy
metadata:
  name: block-dev
  namespace: prod
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: {app: payments}
  action: DENY
  rules:
  - from:
    - source:
        namespaces: ["dev"]
# any ALLOW for dev is irrelevant; the request gets 403 RBAC: access denied

prompt: You are enabling locality load balancing so that `catalog` clients in zone `eu-west-1a` prefer endpoints in the same zone before spilling over. Which statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
options: Locality is derived from the node labels `topology.kubernetes.io/region` and `topology.kubernetes.io/zone`
Locality failover requires `outlierDetection` to be configured in the `DestinationRule`, otherwise Envoy cannot tell when a locality is unhealthy
`localityLbSetting.distribute` lets you send fixed percentages of traffic to specific localities
Locality load balancing only works with the `ROUND_ROBIN` algorithm
Setting `localityLbSetting.enabled: false` in the `DestinationRule` disables it for that host even if the mesh default is on
optionNotes: Correct: istiod reads the standard Kubernetes topology labels (and optional `topology.istio.io/subzone`) from the node and attaches the locality to each endpoint.
Correct: without outlier detection Envoy never marks endpoints unhealthy, so priority failover to another locality never triggers; the docs call this out explicitly.
Correct: `distribute` maps a source locality to a weighted set of destination localities, for example 70% local and 30% to a neighbouring zone.
Wrong: locality-aware routing works with the priority-based load balancers including `ROUND_ROBIN`, `LEAST_REQUEST`, and `RANDOM`; only the algorithm choice is orthogonal.
Correct: the `DestinationRule` field overrides the mesh-wide `localityLbSetting` for that host.
explanation: Locality load balancing is enabled by default in Istio, but failover between localities is only effective when endpoints can be marked unhealthy through `outlierDetection`. `failover` and `distribute` are mutually exclusive ways to shape the behaviour, and `failoverPriority` can add custom label-based ordering.
example:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: catalog
spec:
  host: catalog.shop.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      localityLbSetting:
        enabled: true
        failover:
        - from: eu-west-1
          to: eu-central-1
    outlierDetection:
      consecutive5xxErrors: 3
      interval: 5s
      baseEjectionTime: 1m
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["client in eu-west-1a"] -->|"priority 0"| A["catalog eu-west-1a"]
    C -->|"priority 1"| B["catalog eu-west-1b"]
    C -->|"priority 2 failover"| D["catalog eu-central-1"]
    OD["outlierDetection marks A unhealthy"] -.-> C

prompt: You run two control plane revisions, `1-25` and `1-26`. Forty namespaces are labelled `istio.io/rev=prod-stable`, and `istioctl tag list` shows `prod-stable` pointing at `1-25`. What is the least disruptive way to move all forty namespaces to `1-26`?
options: Run `istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-26`, then restart workloads namespace by namespace
Relabel each namespace to `istio.io/rev=1-26` with a script, then restart workloads
Run `istioctl upgrade --revision 1-26`, which migrates all namespaces automatically
Delete the `1-25` istiod Deployment so the webhook falls back to `1-26`
optionNotes: Correct: revision tags are a stable indirection; repointing the tag updates the mutating webhook so new Pods in tagged namespaces get the `1-26` proxy, with no namespace label changes needed.
This works but is exactly the churn that tags exist to avoid; forty label edits also make rollback slower.
`istioctl upgrade` performs an in-place upgrade of one revision; it does not repoint tags or relabel namespaces.
Deleting istiod does not change which webhook matches the namespace label; injection for those namespaces would fail and existing Pods would lose their control plane.
explanation: `istioctl tag set <tag> --revision <rev>` creates or updates a `MutatingWebhookConfiguration` named `istio-revision-tag-<tag>` that matches `istio.io/rev=<tag>`. Switching a tag is a one-command canary promotion (and rollback), after which you restart workloads to pick up the new proxy; the `default` tag additionally makes a revision handle `istio-injection=enabled`.
example:
istioctl tag list
# TAG          REVISION  NAMESPACES
# prod-stable  1-25      billing,checkout,...
istioctl tag set prod-stable --revision 1-26 --overwrite
kubectl rollout restart deployment -n billing
istioctl proxy-status | grep billing   # proxies now report istiod-1-26
diagram:
flowchart LR
    NS["namespace label\nistio.io/rev=prod-stable"] --> WH["MutatingWebhookConfiguration\nistio-revision-tag-prod-stable"]
    WH -.->|"before"| A["istiod-1-25"]
    WH -->|"after tag set"| B["istiod-1-26"]
    B --> POD["restarted pods get 1.26 proxy"]

prompt: An `EnvoyFilter` is the recommended, API-stable way to change Envoy behaviour in Istio, and its schema is guaranteed to keep working across Istio upgrades.
explanation: `EnvoyFilter` is a break-glass API: it patches raw Envoy configuration generated by istiod and depends on Envoy's internal filter names and xDS structure, which can change between releases. Istio recommends using higher-level APIs (`VirtualService`, `Telemetry`, `WasmPlugin`, `AuthorizationPolicy` CUSTOM action) wherever possible and testing `EnvoyFilter`s carefully during upgrades.
example:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1alpha3
kind: EnvoyFilter
metadata:
  name: add-header
  namespace: shop
spec:
  workloadSelector:
    labels: {app: web}
  configPatches:
  - applyTo: HTTP_FILTER
    match:
      context: SIDECAR_INBOUND
      listener:
        filterChain:
          filter:
            name: envoy.filters.network.http_connection_manager
            subFilter: {name: envoy.filters.http.router}
    patch:
      operation: INSERT_BEFORE
      value: {name: envoy.lua, typed_config: {...}}
diagram:
flowchart LR
    CR["VirtualService, Telemetry, WasmPlugin"] --> I["istiod generates xDS"]
    EF["EnvoyFilter patch\n(applied last, version sensitive)"] --> I
    I --> E["envoy"]

prompt: You want to add a custom authorization header check to the ingress gateway using a WebAssembly module hosted in an OCI registry, without writing an `EnvoyFilter`. Which resource should you use?
options: `WasmPlugin` with `url: oci://registry.example.com/authz-filter:v1` and a `selector` matching the gateway
`Telemetry` with a `providers` entry pointing at the OCI image
`ServiceEntry` with `resolution: DNS` for the registry so Envoy can pull the module
`RequestAuthentication` with `jwtRules.jwksUri` set to the registry URL
optionNotes: Correct: `WasmPlugin` is the first-class API for loading Wasm extensions from `oci://`, `http://`, or `file://` URLs, with `phase` and `priority` to control ordering relative to Istio's built-in filters.
`Telemetry` configures metrics, logs, and tracing providers; it cannot load arbitrary filters.
A `ServiceEntry` only makes a host routable; it does not install any filter into the proxy.
`RequestAuthentication` validates JWTs against a JWKS document; it has no extension mechanism.
explanation: `WasmPlugin` lets istiod distribute Wasm modules to selected proxies. `phase` (`AUTHN`, `AUTHZ`, `STATS`, `UNSPECIFIED_PHASE`) determines where the filter is inserted in the chain, `imagePullSecret` handles private registries, and `pluginConfig` passes configuration to the module.
example:
apiVersion: extensions.istio.io/v1alpha1
kind: WasmPlugin
metadata:
  name: header-authz
  namespace: istio-system
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels: {istio: ingressgateway}
  url: oci://registry.example.com/authz-filter:v1
  imagePullSecret: regcred
  phase: AUTHN
  pluginConfig:
    header: x-api-key
diagram:
flowchart LR
    WP["WasmPlugin CR"] --> I["istiod"]
    REG["OCI registry\nauthz-filter:v1"] --> GW
    I -->|"ECDS config"| GW["ingressgateway envoy"]
    GW --> F["wasm filter in AUTHN phase"]

prompt: Which Prometheus metric emitted by Istio proxies would you query to build a per-service request rate and error rate dashboard?
options: `istio_requests_total`
`envoy_cluster_upstream_cx_total`
`pilot_xds_pushes`
`istio_tcp_sent_bytes_total`
optionNotes: Correct: `istio_requests_total` is the standard HTTP/gRPC request counter with labels such as `destination_service`, `response_code`, `source_workload`, and `connection_security_policy`.
This is a raw Envoy connection counter; it is not labelled with Istio's source and destination dimensions and counts connections rather than requests.
`pilot_xds_pushes` is an istiod control-plane metric about configuration pushes.
`istio_tcp_sent_bytes_total` covers TCP byte volume, not HTTP requests or response codes.
explanation: Istio's standard metrics are `istio_requests_total`, `istio_request_duration_milliseconds`, `istio_request_bytes`, `istio_response_bytes`, and the TCP equivalents. They are generated by the stats filter in each proxy and scraped from port 15020 (merged with app metrics) or 15090.
example:
# request rate to reviews
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service="reviews.default.svc.cluster.local"}[5m]))
# 5xx error ratio
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service="reviews.default.svc.cluster.local",response_code=~"5.."}[5m]))
/
sum(rate(istio_requests_total{destination_service="reviews.default.svc.cluster.local"}[5m]))

    E["envoy stats filter"] --> M["istio_requests_total\nlabels: source, destination, response_code"]
    M -->|"scrape :15020"| P["prometheus"]
    P --> G["grafana / kiali"]

prompt: By default an Istio sidecar imposes no request timeout on HTTP calls, so a `VirtualService` `timeout` is the way to make the client proxy give up on a slow upstream.
explanation: Istio's default HTTP route timeout is disabled (the older default of 15 seconds was removed in 1.7), so a hung upstream can hold a client request indefinitely unless the application sets its own deadline. Setting `timeout` on a `VirtualService` route makes Envoy return 504 after the given duration; note that when retries are configured the timeout is the overall budget, not per attempt.
example:
spec:
  hosts: [ratings]
  http:
  - route:
    - destination: {host: ratings, subset: v1}
    timeout: 3s
    retries:
      attempts: 2
      perTryTimeout: 1s
# curl now gets 504 upstream request timeout after 3s
diagram:
sequenceDiagram
    participant App
    participant Sidecar
    participant Ratings
    App->>Sidecar: GET /ratings
    Sidecar->>Ratings: GET /ratings
    Note over Sidecar: timeout 3s reached
    Sidecar-->>App: 504 upstream request timeout

prompt: You are building a multi-primary, multi-network Istio mesh across two clusters. Which steps are required for cross-cluster traffic to work? (Select all that apply.)
options: Both clusters must share a common root CA so workload certificates issued by each istiod are mutually trusted
An east-west gateway must be deployed in each cluster and exposed with the `istio-system` namespace labelled `topology.istio.io/network`
A remote secret created with `istioctl create-remote-secret` must be applied in each cluster so istiod can watch the other cluster's API server
Every Service must be duplicated as a `ServiceEntry` in the peer cluster
The two clusters must use the same Pod CIDR ranges
optionNotes: Correct: mTLS across clusters only works if each istiod's intermediate CA chains to the same root; sharing the `cacerts` secret is step one in the docs.
Correct: in a multi-network topology Pods cannot reach each other directly, so traffic is routed through an east-west gateway, and the network label tells istiod which endpoints are remote.
Correct: multi-primary requires endpoint discovery in both directions; the remote secret gives istiod credentials for the peer cluster.
Wrong: with endpoint discovery configured, istiod discovers Kubernetes Services in the remote cluster automatically; a Service only needs to exist with the same name and namespace in both clusters.
Wrong: multi-network specifically supports overlapping Pod CIDRs because traffic transits the gateway; only the single-network model needs routable Pod IPs.
explanation: The multi-primary multi-network install combines a shared root CA, network labels, an east-west gateway per cluster (installed via `samples/multicluster/gen-eastwest-gateway.sh`), exposing services through it, and mutual remote secrets for endpoint discovery. Services with the same namespace and name in both clusters are then treated as one service with a merged endpoint set.
example:
# shared CA
kubectl create secret generic cacerts -n istio-system --from-file=certs/ ...
# cluster1
kubectl label ns istio-system topology.istio.io/network=network1
istioctl install --set values.global.meshID=mesh1 --set values.global.multiCluster.clusterName=cluster1 --set values.global.network=network1
samples/multicluster/gen-eastwest-gateway.sh --network network1 | istioctl install -y -f -
kubectl apply -n istio-system -f samples/multicluster/expose-services.yaml
istioctl create-remote-secret --name=cluster2 --context=cluster2 | kubectl apply -f - --context=cluster1

    subgraph C1["cluster1 network1"]
      I1["istiod"]
      A["app A"]
      EW1["east-west gateway"]
    end
    subgraph C2["cluster2 network2"]
      I2["istiod"]
      B["app B"]
      EW2["east-west gateway"]
    end

    A -->|"mTLS via gateway"| EW2
    EW2 --> B

prompt: A Pod's application container starts before the sidecar is ready and its first outbound call to a database fails with a connection error, causing a crash loop. Which setting makes the app container wait until the proxy is up?
options: `holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts: true` in the mesh `defaultConfig` or the `proxy.istio.io/config` Pod annotation
`sidecar.istio.io/inject: "false"` on the Pod
`traffic.sidecar.istio.io/excludeOutboundPorts` set to the database port
A `PeerAuthentication` in `PERMISSIVE` mode for the namespace
optionNotes: Correct: this option injects the proxy as the first container with a `postStart` hook that blocks (or, in newer Istio with native sidecars, uses the Kubernetes init-container sidecar mechanism) so the app only starts once Envoy is serving.
Disabling injection removes the sidecar entirely, so the workload leaves the mesh; it does not fix ordering.
Excluding the port bypasses the proxy for that traffic, losing mTLS and telemetry; it is a workaround rather than a fix.
mTLS mode has no effect on container startup ordering.
explanation: Kubernetes historically started all containers concurrently, so an app could send traffic before Envoy was listening. `holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts` reorders containers and adds a blocking `postStart` hook. On Kubernetes 1.29 and later with the `SidecarContainers` feature, Istio can instead inject the proxy as a native sidecar via `ENABLE_NATIVE_SIDECARS`, which solves both startup and shutdown ordering.
example:
# per-Pod annotation
metadata:
  annotations:
    proxy.istio.io/config: |
      holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts: true

# or mesh-wide
istioctl install --set meshConfig.defaultConfig.holdApplicationUntilProxyStarts=true
diagram:
flowchart LR
    P["pod start"] --> PR["istio-proxy container\npostStart waits for ready"]
    PR --> APP["app container starts"]
    APP -->|"outbound via proxy"| DB["database"]

prompt: In a `DestinationRule` `trafficPolicy.loadBalancer.simple` field, which value tells Envoy to pick the endpoint with the fewest active requests instead of round-robin?
explanation: `LEAST_REQUEST` (it replaced the older `LEAST_CONN` name, which is still accepted as a deprecated alias) makes Envoy sample two random hosts and choose the one with fewer in-flight requests, which copes better than `ROUND_ROBIN` when endpoints have uneven latency. Other `simple` values are `ROUND_ROBIN`, `RANDOM`, and `PASSTHROUGH`; `consistentHash` is the alternative for session affinity.
example:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: DestinationRule
metadata:
  name: search
spec:
  host: search.shop.svc.cluster.local
  trafficPolicy:
    loadBalancer:
      simple: LEAST_REQUEST
  subsets:
  - name: v1
    labels: {version: v1}
    trafficPolicy:
      loadBalancer:
        consistentHash:
          httpHeaderName: x-user-id
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["client sidecar
LEAST_REQUEST"] --> P1["search pod 1
2 active"]
    C -->|"chosen"| P2["search pod 2
0 active"]
    C --> P3["search pod 3
5 active"]

prompt: A platform team applies a mesh-wide `PeerAuthentication` with `mtls.mode: STRICT` in `istio-system`. Minutes later a legacy batch job running in the `reporting` namespace, which has no sidecar and is not in the mesh, starts failing every call to `orders.shop.svc.cluster.local` with `curl: (56) Recv failure: Connection reset by peer`. The `orders` sidecar access log shows entries with response flags `NR` and `filter_chain_not_found`. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The `orders` sidecar now only accepts mTLS on its inbound listener, and the sidecar-less batch job is sending plaintext that matches no filter chain
The `orders` Service has no `DestinationRule` with `tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL`, so the client cannot negotiate TLS
The `reporting` namespace is missing an `AuthorizationPolicy` that allows traffic to `shop`
The batch job is using HTTP/1.1 while STRICT mode requires HTTP/2
optionNotes: Correct. STRICT removes the plaintext filter chain from the inbound listener; a client without a sidecar cannot present a mesh certificate, so Envoy finds no matching filter chain (`NR`) and resets the connection.
Auto mTLS handles the client side for meshed workloads without a `DestinationRule`; the client here has no sidecar at all, so no `DestinationRule` would help it.
A missing `AuthorizationPolicy` produces an HTTP 403 `RBAC: access denied`, not a TCP-level reset with `filter_chain_not_found`.
STRICT mTLS is about transport security, not the HTTP version; HTTP/1.1 works fine over mTLS.
explanation: `filter_chain_not_found` with the `NR` flag on the server sidecar is the signature of plaintext arriving at a listener that only has an mTLS filter chain. The batch job has no sidecar, so it cannot participate in mTLS; the least risky fix is a workload-scoped `PeerAuthentication` for `orders` (or its port) set to `PERMISSIVE` until the caller is onboarded, or onboarding the caller into the mesh.
example:
# confirm the effective mode for the orders workload
istioctl x describe pod orders-7c9d6-abc12 -n shop

# temporary exception while reporting is migrated
apiVersion: security.istio.io/v1
kind: PeerAuthentication
metadata:
  name: orders-permissive
  namespace: shop
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: orders
  mtls:
    mode: PERMISSIVE
diagram:
flowchart LR
    J["batch job (no sidecar)"] -->|"plaintext"| S["orders sidecar inbound listener"]
    S -->|"STRICT: only mTLS chain"| N["NR filter_chain_not_found"]
    N --> R["connection reset"]
    F["fix: PERMISSIVE for orders or onboard the job"] -.-> S

prompt: You add an `AuthorizationPolicy` to the `payments` workload allowing only `source.principals: ["cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/checkout"]`. Immediately every call from `checkout` fails with HTTP 403 and body `RBAC: access denied`. Both workloads have sidecars and `istioctl x describe pod` reports mTLS `STRICT` on `payments`. Running `kubectl get pod -n shop -l app=checkout -o jsonpath='{.items[0].spec.serviceAccountName}'` prints `default`. What is the best fix?
options: Set `serviceAccountName: checkout` in the `checkout` Deployment (creating the ServiceAccount if needed) and roll the pods
Change the policy to `action: DENY` so that the rule only blocks non-matching callers
Switch `payments` to `PeerAuthentication` mode `PERMISSIVE` so the principal check is skipped
Add `source.namespaces: ["shop"]` to the same rule so either condition matches
optionNotes: Correct. The SPIFFE identity is derived from the pod's ServiceAccount; the pods run as `default`, so their principal is `cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/default` and does not match. Running them under the intended ServiceAccount makes the identity match the policy.
A DENY policy that lists the `checkout` principal would block the intended caller once its identity is fixed, and would allow everyone else; it inverts the intent.
PERMISSIVE only changes what the server accepts on the wire; the sidecars still use mTLS between each other and the principal still evaluates to `sa/default`, so the 403 persists.
Fields inside one `from.source` block are ANDed, not ORed, so the request would still need to match the wrong principal. It also weakens the policy to a namespace check.
explanation: Istio derives the peer principal `cluster.local/ns/<ns>/sa/<serviceaccount>` from the client certificate, which is issued per ServiceAccount. Since the `checkout` pods run as the `default` ServiceAccount, the policy's exact principal never matches and Envoy's RBAC filter returns 403. Assigning the intended ServiceAccount is the correct, least privileged fix.
example:
# see what principal the server actually sees
kubectl logs payments-5f8b7-xyz -c istio-proxy -n shop | grep 'rbac'
# ... "RBAC: access denied" peer=spiffe://cluster.local/ns/shop/sa/default

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: checkout
  namespace: shop
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: checkout
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["checkout pod (sa: default)"] -->|"mTLS cert: ns/shop/sa/default"| P["payments sidecar RBAC filter"]
    P -->|"expects ns/shop/sa/checkout"| X["403 RBAC: access denied"]
    F["fix: serviceAccountName: checkout"] -.-> C

prompt: A developer labels the `inventory` namespace with `istio-injection=enabled` and restarts the Deployment, but `kubectl get pods` still shows `1/1` containers and `istioctl proxy-status` does not list the pods. The cluster was installed with `istioctl install --revision 1-26` and `istioctl tag list` prints nothing. What is the most likely cause?
options: The control plane is revisioned and no `default` tag exists, so the `istio-injection=enabled` label does not match any injection webhook
The sidecar injector only runs on pod creation, so the Deployment must be deleted and recreated rather than restarted
The namespace label must be `istio-injection=true` in recent Istio versions
The `istiod` pod is not ready, so the mutating webhook was skipped with `failurePolicy: Ignore`
optionNotes: Correct. A revisioned install registers a webhook that matches `istio.io/rev=1-26`; `istio-injection=enabled` is served only by the `default` revision or a `default` tag, which does not exist here. Use `istio.io/rev=1-26` or run `istioctl tag set default --revision 1-26`.
A rollout restart creates brand-new pods, which is exactly when the injection webhook runs; recreating the Deployment changes nothing.
`istio-injection=enabled` remains the correct value; `true` is not recognized.
The webhook does use `failurePolicy: Fail` by default, and a missing pod would show as pending or failing, not as a clean `1/1` pod.
explanation: With a revisioned control plane, the mutating webhook's namespace selector matches `istio.io/rev=<revision>`, not the legacy `istio-injection=enabled` label, unless a `default` tag points at that revision. `istioctl check-inject` on a pod shows which webhooks matched. Either relabel the namespace with `istio.io/rev=1-26` or create the `default` tag so the legacy label works.
example:
istioctl check-inject -n inventory deploy/inventory
# WEBHOOK                          REVISION  INJECTED
# istio-sidecar-injector-1-26      1-26      ✘

# option A: revision label
kubectl label ns inventory istio-injection- istio.io/rev=1-26
# option B: make 1-26 serve the legacy label
istioctl tag set default --revision 1-26
kubectl rollout restart deploy/inventory -n inventory
diagram:
flowchart TD
    L["ns label istio-injection=enabled"] --> W{"webhook for default revision or tag?"}
    W -->|"none: only rev 1-26"| N["no sidecar injected"]
    W -->|"tag default -> 1-26"| Y["sidecar injected"]
    F["fix: istioctl tag set default or istio.io/rev=1-26"] -.-> W

prompt: Requests to `https://shop.example.com/api` through the ingress gateway return `404 Not Found` with no upstream in the gateway access log. The `Gateway` named `shop-gw` lives in `istio-system` with `hosts: ["shop.example.com"]`, and the `VirtualService` in namespace `shop` has `hosts: ["shop.example.com"]` and `gateways: ["shop-gw"]`. `istioctl analyze -n shop` reports `IST0101 Referenced gateway not found: "shop-gw"`. Which changes would each, on their own, make the route apply? (Select all that apply.)
options: Change the `VirtualService` to `gateways: ["istio-system/shop-gw"]`
Create the `Gateway` resource in the `shop` namespace with the same `selector` and hosts
Add `mesh` to the `gateways` list of the `VirtualService`
Restart the `istio-ingressgateway` Deployment to force a config reload
Change the `VirtualService` `hosts` to `["*"]`
optionNotes: Correct. A bare gateway name resolves in the VirtualService's own namespace; qualifying it as `istio-system/shop-gw` points at the existing Gateway.
Correct. Gateway resources select proxies by label, so a Gateway in `shop` selecting `istio: ingressgateway` configures the same proxy, and the unqualified reference then resolves locally.
`mesh` binds the route to sidecars for in-mesh traffic; it does nothing for the ingress gateway and the reference to `shop-gw` would still be dangling.
The gateway proxy is already synced with istiod; the problem is a config reference that does not resolve, so a restart reproduces the same 404.
Wildcard hosts do not change gateway binding, and would also be rejected unless the Gateway allows those hosts; the missing gateway reference is the actual fault.
explanation: An unqualified entry in `spec.gateways` is looked up in the VirtualService's namespace, so `shop-gw` resolves to `shop/shop-gw`, which does not exist, and the gateway falls through to its default 404 route. Either qualify the reference with the namespace or place the Gateway resource where the short name resolves.
example:
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: shop
  namespace: shop
spec:
  hosts:
  - shop.example.com
  gateways:
  - istio-system/shop-gw
  http:
  - match:
    - uri:
        prefix: /api
    route:
    - destination:
        host: api.shop.svc.cluster.local

# verify the route landed on the gateway
istioctl proxy-config routes deploy/istio-ingressgateway -n istio-system --name https.443.https.shop-gw.istio-system
diagram:
flowchart LR
    U["client shop.example.com/api"] --> G["ingress gateway"]
    G -->|"lookup shop/shop-gw"| M["no VirtualService bound"]
    M --> E["404 Not Found"]
    F["fix: gateways: istio-system/shop-gw"] -.-> G

prompt: The `catalog` Service exposes port 8080 with `name: api`. In Kiali the edge from `frontend` to `catalog` is drawn as a TCP connection, `istio_requests_total` has no series for `catalog`, and the `VirtualService` retry and header-match rules for `catalog` are ignored. Envoy access logs on the client show a plain TCP proxy entry. What is the most likely cause?
options: The Service port name `api` does not declare a protocol, and sniffing was disabled, so Istio treats the port as opaque TCP
The `catalog` pods are missing the `version` label required for HTTP telemetry
The `VirtualService` must be in the `istio-system` namespace to affect sidecar traffic
The client sidecar is not `SYNCED` with istiod and holds stale configuration
optionNotes: Correct. Istio decides the L7 protocol from the port name prefix (`http-`, `grpc-`, `http2-`, `tcp-`) or the `appProtocol` field. With neither and sniffing off, the port is TCP, so HTTP metrics, retries and header routing do not apply.
Labels feed the `destination_version` label but do not gate whether HTTP telemetry is generated at all.
VirtualServices apply from any namespace; namespace placement does not turn TCP into HTTP.
A stale proxy would show mismatched config, but the client log is a TCP proxy entry that matches the current config, which means the listener really is TCP.
explanation: Envoy only applies HTTP routing, retries and L7 telemetry when the listener is configured as an HTTP connection manager, and Istio selects that from the Service port's protocol. Rename the port to `http-api` (or set `appProtocol: http`) so istiod programs an HTTP listener; the difference is visible in `istioctl proxy-config listeners`.
example:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: catalog
  namespace: shop
spec:
  ports:
  - name: http-api        # or keep name: api and add appProtocol: http
    port: 8080
    targetPort: 8080

istioctl proxy-config listeners deploy/frontend -n shop --port 8080
# before: ... Cluster: outbound|8080||catalog.shop.svc.cluster.local (TCP)
# after:  ... Route: 8080 (HTTP)
diagram:
flowchart LR
    P["Service port name: api"] --> D{"protocol known?"}
    D -->|"no"| T["TCP listener: no retries, no L7 metrics"]
    D -->|"http-api or appProtocol"| H["HTTP listener: VirtualService rules apply"]

prompt: A `VirtualService` for `report-generator` sets `timeout: 10s` and `retries: {attempts: 2, perTryTimeout: 8s}`. The application itself is configured to allow 60 seconds per report and callers now see `504` with response flag `UT` after roughly 10 seconds. True or false: the `504 UT` comes from the client sidecar's route timeout, which caps the total time including all retry attempts, so raising the application's own 60 second limit will not change the observed behaviour.
explanation: `UT` (upstream request timeout) is set by the calling Envoy when the route `timeout` expires; that timeout is the overall budget across the original attempt and every retry, and `perTryTimeout` only bounds a single attempt within it. The server-side limit never comes into play because the client proxy abandons the request first, so the fix is to raise or disable the `VirtualService` timeout (for example `timeout: 90s`) or move slow reports to an asynchronous path.
example:
# client sidecar access log
[2026-09-11T02:14:07Z] "POST /reports HTTP/1.1" 504 UT ... 10001 - "-" "report-generator.shop.svc.cluster.local:8080"

apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata:
  name: report-generator
spec:
  hosts: [report-generator]
  http:
  - timeout: 90s
    retries:
      attempts: 2
      perTryTimeout: 40s
      retryOn: connect-failure,refused-stream
    route:
    - destination:
        host: report-generator
diagram:
flowchart LR
    C["caller"] --> S["client sidecar route timeout 10s"]
    S -->|"attempt 1 (8s)"| A["report-generator (needs 60s)"]

prompt: You roll out `reviews-v3` behind a `VirtualService` weighting `v1: 90` and `v3: 10`. The `DestinationRule` defines subset `v3` with `labels: {version: v3}` and `istioctl analyze` is clean. After the change, roughly 10% of requests fail with HTTP 503 and response flag `UH`, and `istioctl proxy-config endpoints deploy/productpage --cluster "outbound|9080|v3|reviews.shop.svc.cluster.local"` prints no rows. What is the most likely root cause?
options: The `reviews-v3` pods do not carry the `version: v3` label, so the subset cluster has no endpoints
The `VirtualService` weights must sum to 100 and the current values are being rounded to 0 for `v3`
The `reviews-v3` Deployment has no sidecar, so Envoy excludes its pods from the mesh registry
Outlier detection ejected all `v3` endpoints after the first failed health check
optionNotes: Correct. `UH` means no healthy upstream in the chosen cluster; an empty endpoint list for the subset cluster while analyze is clean points to the subset selector not matching any pod labels.
The weights already sum to 100; Istio validates the sum and would report a configuration error rather than silently round.
Pods without a sidecar are still Service endpoints and appear in EDS; missing injection causes plaintext or mTLS issues, not an empty subset.

explanation: A subset cluster is populated from Service endpoints whose pod labels match the subset's `labels`. If the new Deployment's pod template lacks `version: v3`, the cluster exists but is empty, so the 10% of requests routed to it get `503 UH` while `istioctl analyze` sees a syntactically valid setup. prompt: A security review requires the `shop` namespace to enforce `STRICT` mTLS by the end of the quarter. Today the namespace is `PERMISSIVE`, and a few callers are VMs and legacy pods outside the mesh. You must reach STRICT without breaking any caller. Which steps belong in a safe migration plan? (Select all that apply.)
options: Query Prometheus for `istio_requests_total{destination_namespace="shop", connection_security_policy="none"}` to identify callers still sending plaintext
Onboard the plaintext callers (inject sidecars, or add VMs via `WorkloadEntry`) before changing the mode
Apply a namespace-scoped `PeerAuthentication` with `mode: STRICT` in `shop` rather than a mesh-wide one, then watch for `NR` errors
Create a `DestinationRule` with `tls.mode: ISTIO_MUTUAL` for every Service in `shop` so clients start using mTLS
Switch the mesh-wide policy to `STRICT` first, then fix whichever callers break
optionNotes: Correct. The server-side `connection_security_policy` label is `none` for plaintext requests, which gives you an inventory of callers that STRICT would break.
Correct. STRICT requires every client to present a mesh certificate, so the non-mesh callers must be brought into the mesh (or given a scoped exception) before the switch.
Correct. Scoping the policy to the namespace limits the blast radius, and monitoring the `NR` response flag on server sidecars catches any caller you missed.

With auto mTLS, meshed clients already use mTLS toward sidecar-backed destinations; forcing `ISTIO_MUTUAL` in a DestinationRule is unnecessary and breaks calls to any destination that still lacks a sidecar.
A mesh-wide STRICT switch is the highest-risk option and affects every namespace, including ones that were not part of the requirement.
explanation: The safe path is to measure plaintext traffic while still PERMISSIVE, onboard or exempt every plaintext caller, and only then tighten the policy at the smallest scope that meets the requirement. Auto mTLS already upgrades meshed clients, so DestinationRule changes are not part of the server-side enforcement story.

metadata:

  namespace: shop
